title: Ordering food without misunderstandings
title_target: สั่งอาหาร — Sàng aa-hǎan
goal: Order at a street stall or a restaurant, set the spice level, ask for something to be left out, and ask for the bill — including the phrases Muslim, vegetarian, and pork-free diners especially need.

dialogs.intro: Budi and Nok are having lunch. Notice how one small word — ใส่ (to put in) — saves the whole meal for anyone with dietary restrictions.

notes: **ขอ khǎaw and เอา ao both mean "I'll have", but they feel different.** *ขอ* is softer and fits anything; *เอา* is more direct and very common at street stalls. A safe rule: use *ขอ* for small things (the menu, water, a spoon) and *เอา* for ordering dishes. Both are polite as long as they end with *ครับ/ค่ะ*.

**ที่ thîi is the classifier for a SERVING of food**, not just "place". *ต้มยำหนึ่งที่* = one serving of tom yam. For dishes served on a plate, *จาน jaan* is also correct. Both sound natural; *ที่* is a little more flexible.

**ใส่ sài means "to put in", and ไม่ใส่ is the key to every dietary restriction.** *ไม่ใส่หมู* (no pork), *ไม่ใส่ผงชูรส* (no MSG), *ไม่ใส่น้ำปลา* (no fish sauce), *ไม่ใส่น้ำตาล* (no sugar). This one pattern solves more problems than any list of food vocabulary.

**Spice levels have their own ladder**, and you'd better start at the bottom: *ไม่เผ็ด mâi phèt* (not spicy) → *เผ็ดนิดหน่อย phèt nít-nàwy* (a little spicy) → *เผ็ดน้อย phèt náwy* (mildly spicy) → *เผ็ดปกติ phèt pà-kà-tì* (normal spicy) → *เผ็ดมาก phèt mâak* (very spicy). ⚠️ "Normal spicy" in Thailand is often "very spicy" by most foreigners' standards, especially for *ส้มตำ* and Isan food.

**ไม่ค่อย mâi khâwy means "not really", and it softens a refusal.** *เผ็ดไม่ค่อยได้* = "I can't really handle spicy food". This is much gentler than *ไม่ได้*, which sounds blunt. Thai loves softened forms like this; Unit 19 explains why.

**เช็คบิล chék-bin means "check, please"**, borrowed from English *check bill* and used everywhere. The native Thai form is *คิดเงินด้วยครับ khít-ngoen dûai khráp* (literally "please count the money"), which is actually more common at simple stalls.
**ท่าน thâan is an honorific word for "person"**, used by restaurant, airport, and office staff. You don't need to use it yourself — just understand it when you hear it. Answer with plain *คน khon*.

**อิ่ม ìm means full, and it's an adjective — so no "to be" is needed.** *อิ่มแล้วครับ* = I'm full. Its opposite is *หิว hǐu* (hungry). These two words, plus *อร่อย*, are enough to give complete feedback on any meal.

after: Thai dish names follow a very regular pattern: **cooking method + ingredient**. *ผัด phàt* = stir-fry, *ต้ม tôm* = boil, *ทอด thâwt* = deep-fry, *ย่าง yâang* = grill, *นึ่ง nûeng* = steam, *แกง kaaeng* = curry. Combine with *ไก่ kài* (chicken), *หมู mǔu* (pork), *เนื้อ núuea* (beef), *กุ้ง kûng* (shrimp), *ปลา plaa* (fish), *ผัก phàk* (vegetables) — and you can read half the menu without ever memorizing it.

sections.title: For Muslim readers and anyone avoiding pork: phrases to learn

blocks.text: Thailand has a sizable Muslim population, especially in the south, and the terms are widely understood in big cities. What you need to watch for isn't visible pork, but the **broth and seasonings** you can't see.

blocks.title: Three practical tips
items: **Look for the green ฮาลาล (haa-laan) sign** on the stall's window. In Bangkok, the Nana area, Ramkhamhaeng, and the area around the Java Mosque have plenty of options.

**กินเจ *kin jee* is your magic word when in doubt.** It means strict vegan in the Chinese-Thai tradition: no meat, no animal broth, not even garlic or onion. Stalls with a yellow flag marked เจ are guaranteed pork-free.

⚠️ **น้ำปลา *náam-plaa* (fish sauce) is in almost every Thai dish**, which isn't a problem for most people — but *ผัดกะเพรา* and *ก๋วยเตี๋ยว* very often use pork broth without saying so. Asking *ใส่หมูไหมคะ/ครับ* before you order is safer than guessing from how it looks.

head: Thai
Pronunciation
English
rows: ร้อน / เย็น

blocks.text: To compliment someone's cooking, the best phrase isn't just *อร่อย* but **อร่อยมากครับ/ค่ะ** or **อร่อยจัง** — both sound sincere. If someone asks *เผ็ดไหม* and you're overwhelmed, the safest answer is *เผ็ดนิดหน่อยครับ/ค่ะ* with a smile; your host will hand you water rather than feel offended.

blocks.title: "กินข้าวหรือยัง" is not an invitation to eat
items: *กินข้าวหรือยัง kin khâao rǔue yang* — "have you eaten yet?" — is a greeting, not an invitation. Thais use it exactly as English speakers use "how's it going?".

There are only two standard answers: *กินแล้วครับ/ค่ะ kin láaeo* (yes, I have) or *ยังครับ/ค่ะ yang* (not yet). If you answer "not yet", there's a real chance you'll actually be invited to eat — and turning that down takes skills covered in Unit 19.
